en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 6.
The Training Rule on Requesting from Strangers:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan was skilled in giving a Dhamma talk.
Then a certain son of a merchant approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that son of a merchant with a Dhamma talk.
Then the merchant’s son, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan with a discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan:
“Venerable sir, please say what you need.
We are capable of providing for the Master whatever is required: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“If you wish to give to me, friend, give me one of these garments.
“Venerable sir, for us sons of good family, how could we go about with only a single garment?
Wait, venerable sir, until I have gone home.”
“Having gone home, I will send back either one garment from here or something more beautiful.
A second time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son said this to that merchant’s son:
“If you wish to give me something, friend, give me one garment from here.”

“Venerable sir, for us sons of good family it would be like going about with only a single garment; wait, venerable sir, until I go home. Once I have reached home, I will send back one garment from there, or perhaps something more beautiful.
A third time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son said this to that merchant’s son:
“If you wish to give me, friend, then give me one garment from there.”

“Venerable sir, for us sons of good family, it is as if we must go about with only a single garment. Please wait, venerable sir, until I have gone home; once I have reached home, I will send one garment from there, or perhaps something even more beautiful.
“But friend, why did you not give what you had invited [us] to give when you were pressed by him?
Then that son of a merchant, being pressured by the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son, gave him one garment and departed.
People said to that merchant’s son, “Noble sir, why are you coming with only a single robe?
Then the merchant’s son explained the matter to those people.
The people criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, have great desires and are not content.
It is not easy even to invite them to the Dhamma.
For how could they accept a garment when an invitation to the Dhamma is being offered by the merchant’s son?”
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized, saying:
"How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son request a robe from the merchant’s son?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, Upananda, that you requested a robe from the merchant’s son?
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
“Upananda, is he a kinsman of yours or not a kinsman?
“He is not a kinsman, Blessed One.
“An unrelated person, foolish man, does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is real or unreal, regarding another who is unrelated.”
"In this matter, foolish man, you have asked an unrelated son of a merchant for a robe.
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whichever monk, however, should request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a number of monks were traveling on the highway from Sāketa to Sāvatthī. On the way, bandits came out and robbed those monks.
Then those bhikkhus, thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited asking an unrelated householder or housewife for a robe,” being afraid of wrongdoing, did not ask for one.
They went to Sāvatthī naked and paid homage to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus said, “These Ājīvakas are indeed handsome, friends, who pay homage to these bhikkhus.”
They replied, “We are not Ājīvakas, friends; we are bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus said to the Venerable Upāli, “Come now, friend Upāli, you must question these men. Then, while being questioned by the Venerable Upāli, those bhikkhus reported this matter to him. Then...
After questioning those monks, the Venerable Upāli said to the monks, “Friends, these are monks. Give them their robes.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying, “How can these monks come naked?”
“Surely one should come having covered [the body] with grass or leaves.
Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, when your robe has been cut off or lost, to ask an unrelated householder or housewife for a robe.

If he first enters a certain residence and there is a robe belonging to the Sangha—whether it be a dwelling-robe, an upper-blanket, a floor-covering, or a mattress-cover—he may take it and put it on, thinking: ‘Having obtained it, I will return it.’”

If there is no robe belonging to the Saṅgha in the monastery—whether it be an upper robe, a sheet for spreading out, a rug for the floor, or a mattress cover—one should not return having covered oneself with grass or leaves; one must certainly not return naked.
Whoever should so return commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whatever monk should request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the monk is either without a robe or his robe has been lost.
This is the appropriate occasion therein.”
"But whoever" means whoever of such a kind... "monks" means... [as before]... monks.
... [as before] ... this is the meaning intended here by "bhikkhu.
One who is unrelated (*aññātaka*) means one who is not connected by descent from the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation on the paternal line.
A householder (*gahapati*) is anyone who dwells in a home.
A housewife (*gahapatānī*) is...
Whoever dwells in a house.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes that is suitable for assignment and is of the lowest quality.
"Except at the proper time" means excluding the proper time.
"One whose robes have been stolen" means:
A monk’s robe has been stolen by kings, thieves, rogues, or by anyone at all.
A monk is said to have lost his robes when his robe has been burnt by fire, swept away by water, gnawed by rats or termites, or worn out through use.
If she requests it except on an appropriate occasion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of requesting.
Upon obtaining it, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:
… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth, belonging to an unrelated householder, was requested by me outside of the proper occasion; it is to be relinquished.”
"I relinquish this to the Saṅgha" ...
"let him give it" ...
"let them give it" ... [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.

If he requests a robe from one who is not related, perceiving that person as not related, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If he requests a robe from one who is not related, being in doubt about whether they are related, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If one asks for a robe from someone who is not a relative, perceiving them as a relative, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one asks for a robe from a relative, perceiving them as not a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one has doubt regarding a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense at the proper time.
[It is not an offense] for relatives,
for those who have invited [one to eat],
or for the sake of another.
With one's own wealth;
for one who is insane;
for the first offender.
The sixth training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person is finished.
